title: Krishna Departs Hastinapura
subtitle: A city watches its friend leave
story:
It was months before Krishna could bring himself to leave Hastinapura.

He had stayed on after the great war — to gladden his friends, to comfort his sister Subhadra, who mourned the dead of two houses, to let a broken city begin to heal in the presence of someone it trusted completely. The months passed, the wounds of the Kuru house began to close, and still the parting was put off. At last it could be delayed no longer. He took leave of everyone, embraced them one by one, bowed to the elders, and mounted his chariot. The morning was clear, and every person in the city knew this was the last they would see of him from their own streets for a long while.

And the city could not let him go.

Subhadra, Draupadi, Kunti — Gandhari, Dhritarashtra, all of them — could not bear the thought of his going. Their eyes followed him and would not turn away. The wise, the verses say, once they have tasted true company, cannot give it up again; how then could the Pandavas, whose minds were fixed on Krishna, endure his absence? Tears rose in their eyes and were held back, from sheer longing for Devaki's son. No one wanted to be the first to look away.

The whole city came out to see him go. The mridangas sounded and the conches, the bheris and the vinas; drums and horns answered down the length of the royal road. The women of the Kuru house climbed to the roofs of the palaces, desperate for one more sight of him, and the children of the city ran beside the chariot wheels until the road turned. A white umbrella sewn with pearl garlands was raised over his head, and Uddhava and Satyaki walked beside his chariot, waving the great chauris. Here and there along the way, the blessings of the brahmins rose over the noise and were heard.

And as the chariot moved through the streets, the people spoke to one another of the one who was leaving. "This is he, surely," they said — "the ancient Person, who alone existed before all distinctions, who by his own power sets creation turning again. His are the feet the sages seek; his deeds are sung in the hidden places of the Vedas. When kings grow dark with unrighteousness, he comes down." "How praiseworthy is the clan of Yadu," others said, "how holy the forest of Madhu that raised him. And Kushasthali, his city — it dims the glory of heaven itself and makes the earth famous. The women who won him by the price of valor, carrying off the fierce king of Chedi and the rest at the svayamvara, make womanhood itself glorious." So the women of the city talked as he passed. The verses set it down that these were the words heard along the royal road that morning — a whole city praising, as one, the one it loved.

Yudhishthira rode with him part of the way, for the protection of the army and the escort. And there at the edge of the city, the Kurus stood at a distance, tormented by separation, their eyes unblinking on the figure growing smaller down the road.

Krishna passed on. He travelled through Kuru-jangala and Panchala, through Shurasena and the lands along the Yamuna, across the Maru desert, through the far reaches of Sauvira and Abhira. And at every kingdom he crossed, the people came out to meet him and did him honor, pressing gifts upon him as he passed — for the road to Dwaraka, though long, ran through a country that had been waiting to see him.
reflection: The verses pause to note that those who have known such company cannot bear to lose it, and the Pandavas, whose minds were fixed on Krishna, could hardly endure the parting. What makes the scene moving is that the grief is not for a king or a deity but for a friend: the city grieves him as a presence that will simply be gone.
next_story_tease: Ahead lay the desert road — and a sea-girt city already decking its gates for his return.
hero_scene: Krishna's chariot rolling out of Hastinapura beneath a white umbrella sewn with pearls, Uddhava and Satyaki waving great fans on either side, while the women of the Kuru house watch from the palace roofs and the Pandavas stand at the city's edge, unable to look away.
